# INTRODUCTION

salmonMSE is a stochastic decision-support tool for Pacific salmon focusing on strategic trade-offs among harvest, hatchery and habitat management levers.
salmonMSE can be used for risk-based analyses to evaluate the performance, prioritize management actions and identify trade-offs towards achieving biological and harvest objectives. 
The goal of salmonMSE is to facilitate the implementation of management strategy evaluation (MSE), a framework for simulating and evaluating the outcomes of management procedures, within the stock assessment process for Pacific salmon species.

salmonMSE is a generalizable tool applicable across salmon species and populations, and expands upon previous simulation tools such as samSim [@holt2020] and AHA [@hsrg2020].
These tools project a simulated population over successive generations to obtain the long-term equilibrium properties of the state dynamics.
To accommodate more complex life histories, salmonMSE is age-structured which is useful for salmon that usually have returns comprising multiple brood-years.
salmonMSE also explicitly models juvenile mortality in freshwater and marine life stage, where this information is available.
Importantly, salmonMSE was developed to comprehensively support evaluation of harvest policies, hatchery enhancement programs, and changes in early freshwater survival, e.g., due to habitat modifications, simultaneously.
Finally, stochasticity can be incorporated in the model to evaluate outcomes across uncertain parameters.
In general, its flexibility is intended to encapsulate a gradient of simple to more complex models as data availability to inform parameters allows.

salmonMSE can be used to address questions such as:

- How does a change in hatchery release strategy impact harvest and conservation objectives?
- How does a candidate broodtake rule impact the ability to achieve PNI and conservation objectives?
- How do changes in environmental drivers impact ability to rebuild populations?
- How do mark-selective fisheries impact harvest and conservation objectives?
- What combination of fishery exploitation rates and hatchery production targets meets spawner abundance objectives?

This document is intended to be a summary of the age-structured projection model in salmonMSE.
The equations are described in the following order:
<!--CH comment: given that we generally think about salmon abundances starting with spawner abundance as these are foundational data, can we start there?  Initially the model was initiated from historical juvenile abundances, but I think it was revised so that it could be initiated with spawners instead, correct Quang?-->
- Juvenile marine abundance in the beginning of the annual time step, followed by preterminal fishing
- Maturation and recruitment of the mature component of the population, followed by terminal fishing
- Escapement from marine fisheries to the in-river return, where there is broodtake for hatchery programs and further in-river removals
- Spawner abundance and egg production
- Survival to outmigrating juveniles of the next generation in the next time step 
<!--CH comment: can this be generalized to outmigrating juveniles, which can occur in the next time-step, or in two time-steps, if salmon stay in fw for 2 years?  Even if the model doesn't include it now, better to omit the age-step here, so that we can add it later.-->
- Advancement of age classes of juveniles that did not mature in the previous time step

A glossary of important state variables is provided in Table \@ref(tab:glossary). 

Appendices describe various modifications to the system dynamics including mark-selective fishing (Appendix \@ref(app:msf)), fitness impacts on juvenile survival from genetic drift due to selection against hatchery traits in the natural environment (Appendix \@ref(app:fitness)), and multi-population models (Appendix \@ref(app:multi)).

# MODEL OVERVIEW

The equations are presented for salmonMSE version 3.1.0.
The corresponding R code is available on Github at [https://github.com/Blue-Matter/salmonMSE](https://github.com/Blue-Matter/salmonMSE).
`ProjectSOM()` is the primary function that executes the projection and calls subsidiary functions that implement different components of the simulation (Table \@ref(tab:equation-table)).
<!--CH comment: Quang, if salmonMSE() is the wrapper function for PRojectSOM, should we use that one here?  Also, salmonMSE() is used below-->

The projection tool uses an operating model to simulate population trajectories and outcomes of management procedures, while incorporating feedback between the two at each timestep (Figure \@ref(fig:overview)). 
The operating model may be parameterized with data and outputs from historical modelling, or values drawn from expert knowledge or literature sources.
The operating model is defined by five components, outlined below: biological, habitat, hatchery, harvest and historical, used to initiate the model.
Outcomes can be summarized with a range of probabilistic performance metrics, such as the probability of exceeding spawner abundance benchmarks or reference points or PNI (proportionate natural influence) thresholds.
salmonMSE can be of particular interest for modelling multiple populations that co-mingle in mixed-stock fisheries, or interact via straying. 
In such cases, the components of the operating model can be defined and simulated across multiple populations simultaneously.

## Biological

The biological component of the operating model specifies the life history parameters of the modelled population(s), including longevity, survival, maturity, fecundity and spawner-recruit parameters.
Survival rates include age-specific natural marine survival and en-route survival prior to spawning in freshwater.
<!--CH: my preference is 'spawner-recruit' instead of stock-recruit everywhere. stock is a utilitarian word associated with fisheries, esp. commercial fisheries, and I prefer the biological word 'spawner' where possible.-->
Spawner-recruit dynamics, used to model density-dependence from the egg to smolt life stages, can be specified through parameters of either a Ricker or Beverton-Holt model. 
The model also contains the flexibility to model multiple life-history groups within a population that vary in natural survival and maturity (see @sorel2023 and @brown2026 for examples in Chinook salmon).

## Habitat

The habitat component contains freshwater survival parameters, used to model the effects of changing environmental and climate conditions, or habitat improvements through mitigations and restoration actions.
Specifying the parameters here allows the user to partition density-dependence in freshwater across the transitions between the spawner, egg, fry and smolt life stages.
Productivity and capacity parameters can be defined for either Beverton-Holt or hockey-stick relationships.
Competition between hatchery releases and natural-origin fish can be modelled as well (see hatchery section below).
Alternatively, freshwater survival survival can be modelled as random deviations independent of density. <!--CH comment: I added this last sentence, correct?-->

## Hatchery

The hatchery component defines parameters related to hatchery management, including hatchery releases and broodstock collection, as well as the characteristics of hatchery-origin fish, including fitness and survival rates that differ from those of natural-origin fish.
The model allows the user to specify a target number of releases and desired proportion of natural-origin spawners in the brood, and calculates broodtake and resulting hatchery production using information on available spawners, fecundity and survival rates of brood and eggs. 
Stray rates can also be included to represent inputs from and losses to other systems.<!-- CH comment: I added 'and losses to', correct?-->
Multiple hatchery release strategies can be modelled, with different survival and maturity rates across strategies.

## Harvest

The harvest component specifies exploitation rates for pre-terminal and terminal fisheries.
Fisheries can either be managed by exploitation rate, or by catch targets, with differential vulnerability to harvest across age classes, allowing the user to model selectivity in the fishery.
A custom harvest control rule can be defined where the target exploitation rate or catch is a function of abundance, subject to observation error and implementation error.
Mark-selective fisheries can also be implemented in either fishery, accounting for mortality rates of released fish. 

## Historical

The historical component contains the historical starting conditions to initialize the simulation.
These can be either fixed values or posterior distributions from an estimation model.<!--CH: I  want to confirm that this box is about initializing the model with 1st year abundances from historical data, and not about parameterizing the OM from  historical data? I added 'to initalize' in the sentence above to make it more clear for me - and would like to confirm that is what was intended.-->

# EXAMPLE CODE

Users specify the parameters of the simulation through an S4 object of class `SOM`, which in itself is comprised of smaller S4 objects (class Bio, Habitat, Hatchery, or Harvest) that organize the biological dynamics and management levers. Generally, an S4 object is formal and structured representation of an object in R that contains slots that can also be S4 objects: 
<!--CH comment: I tried to define S4 object above, please revise as needed. Also, I'm not sure whay Bio<-new("Bio") is included in the example below, but not the others. Can you  add in new Habitat, Hatchery, and Harvest objects, and describe how that line of code creates default objects that have default parameters for each component?-->

```{r, eval=FALSE, echo=TRUE}
Bio <- new("Bio")
SOM <- new(
  "SOM",
  Bio,
  Habitat,
  Hatchery,
  Harvest
)
```

The simulation of the projection model is run with a call to the `salmonMSE()` function:

```{r, eval=FALSE, echo=TRUE}
SMSE <- salmonMSE(SOM)
```

The output is another S4 object, of a class called 'SMSE', that reports the results of the projection.<!--CH: 'of the projection' not 'to the projection', correct?-->
The contents of any S4 objects can be assigned or extracted  with the "@" symbol, for example, assigning the 'kappa', or productivity parameter within the Bio object, or extracting the projected time-series of natural-origin spawners, NOS, from the SMSE results object: <!--CH comment: I just added a description of the code below, to guide the reader a bit. Please revise as necessry -->

```{r, eval=FALSE, echo=TRUE}
Bio@kappa <- 3
SMSE@NOS
```

```{r glossary, results="asis"}
glossary <- readr::read_csv("tables/glossary.csv") %>%
  filter(Type_Internal != "Fitness") %>%
  arrange(Entry) %>%
  select(Name, Definition, Type, Slot)

flextable(glossary) %>%
  compose(j = "Name", value = as_paragraph(as_equation(Name))) %>%
  valign(j = 1:4, valign = "top", part = "all") %>%
  #align(j = 1:4, align = "left", part = "all") %>%
  set_table_properties(layout = "autofit") %>%
  set_caption("Glossary of state variables used in the dynamics equations and their relation to the R code, either as user inputs, internal variables (not reported to user), or reported outputs. Inputs are stored in an S4 object of class SOM and outputs are reported in an S4 object of class SMSE. The table reports the corresponding slots for the state variables in the S4 objects.")
```
